slides.headline: Shave a tiger and it's still striped.
slides.sub: The pattern is in the skin, and no two tigers share one

slides.headline: The stripes go skin-deep
slides.body: Zoo vets who shave a sedated tiger for treatment find the bare skin underneath carries the same stripe pattern as the fur.

slides.headline: No two tigers match
slides.body: Stripes vary in size, length and spacing along the flanks and shoulders. Like a human fingerprint, every tiger's pattern is its own.
slides.source: Smithsonian's National Zoo; Animal Diversity Web

slides.headline: Camera traps count them by their stripes
slides.body: Remote cameras photograph passing tigers. Matching stripe patterns tells individuals apart, so scientists can estimate how many live in a forest.

slides.label: mature tigers estimated left in the wild
slides.body: IUCN's best estimate, within a range of 2,608–3,905. South Asian range states hold about 76% of the global population.

slides.headline: Endangered, and still decreasing
slides.body: The tiger is listed as Endangered (assessed 2021, published 2022) with a decreasing global trend, driven largely by poaching and habitat loss.

slides.headline: Every stripe is a name tag.
slides.body: Save this for the next time someone says all tigers look the same.
sources: IUCN Red List: Panthera tigris (assessed 2021, publ. 2022) iucnredlist.org/species/15955/214862019

caption:
Shave a tiger (Panthera tigris) and the stripes are still there: the pattern is in the skin, and no two tigers share one.

That uniqueness is a research tool. Since the 1990s, camera traps in India have photographed passing tigers and matched their stripes to tell individuals apart, turning photos into population estimates. The tigers in these photos were all photographed in the wild, mostly in Ranthambore National Park, Rajasthan.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List (2022); Karanth & Nichols, Ecology (1998).
